provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: The acts of the apostles
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to state the events of Pentecost, explain the meaning of Spirit power, and identify how the church began.

Introduction:
Last term we learned about the life of Jesus. Today we will see how Jesus' followers started the church after He went to heaven.

Content:
The church was born on the day of Pentecost when the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles. They spoke in different languages as the Spirit gave them ability. Peter preached and 3000 people believed that day. The apostles performed miracles like healing a man who could not walk, just like Jesus did. The early Christians shared everything they had, like when they sold property to help others in need.

Class activity:
Pupils will work in groups to act out the coming of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.

Evaluation questions:
1. What happened on the day of Pentecost?
2. Name one miracle performed by the apostles.
3. How did the Holy Spirit help the apostles?
4. Why is the day of Pentecost important for Christians?

Summary:
The Holy Spirit empowered the apostles to begin the church and spread the gospel message.

topics.title: Missions: Paul's letters
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to list Paul's letters to the churches, explain how Christians encouraged one another, and state the importance of letters in the early church.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about how the church began. Today we will learn about how Paul wrote letters to different churches to teach and encourage them.

Content:
Paul wrote many letters to churches like Rome, Corinth, Ephesus, and Galatia. In these letters, he taught about faith, love, and good behaviour. He encouraged Christians to stand firm in their faith like a strong tree during harmattan wind. Paul told them to love one another as brothers and sisters in a big family. He also reminded them to share with those in need, like sharing food at a Nigerian party.

Class activity:
Pupils will write a short encouraging letter to a friend facing challenges.

Evaluation questions:
1. Name two churches Paul wrote letters to.
2. How did Paul encourage Christians in his letters?
3. What should Christians do according to Paul's teaching?
4. Why are letters important for communication?

Summary:
Paul's letters taught Christians important lessons and helped them stay strong in their faith.

topics.title: Christian persecution
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain what persecution means, identify how Christians stand firm, and tell a story of courage from the Bible.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about Paul's letters to churches. Today we will learn about how some Christians faced difficulties because of their faith.

Content:
Persecution means being treated badly because of what you believe. Early Christians were persecuted for following Jesus. Stephen was stoned to death for preaching about Jesus. Peter and John were arrested for healing a man. Despite these troubles, they stood firm like a strong Iroko tree. Their courage inspired others to keep believing in Jesus, just like our heroes inspire us in Nigeria.

Class activity:
Pupils will role-play a Bible story of persecution and how the Christian responded with courage.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is persecution?
2. Name one person who was persecuted in the Bible.
3. How should Christians respond when persecuted?
4. Why is courage important for Christians?

Summary:
Christians should remain faithful and courageous even when facing persecution for their beliefs.

topics.title: Faith and works
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain James' teaching on faith and works, identify how faith is shown through actions, and differentiate between faith that works and dead faith.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about persecution. Today we will learn that true faith is not just believing but also showing it through our actions.

Content:
James taught that faith without works is dead, like a seed that never grows. He said Abraham showed his faith by obeying God and offering his son Isaac. Rahab showed her faith by helping the spies, and her whole family was saved. True faith is like a mango tree that produces fruit, not just a tree with only leaves. We show our faith by helping others, being honest, and sharing what we have, like sharing your lunch with a hungry classmate.

Class activity:
Pupils will draw pictures showing how they can demonstrate their faith through good actions.

Evaluation questions:
1. What did James say about faith without works?
2. How did Abraham show his faith through actions?
3. Give an example of how you can show your faith at school.
4. Why is it important for faith to lead to action?

Summary:
True faith produces good works that show we really believe in Jesus.

topics.title: The tongue
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain how words can heal or hurt, identify ways to guard speech, and list examples of both helpful and harmful words.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about faith and works. Today we will learn about the power of our words and how we should use them wisely.

Content:
The tongue is small but has great power, like a match that can start a big fire. Words can heal, like when you comfort a friend who lost a parent. Words can also hurt, like when you call someone bad names. The Bible says to speak only what is good and helpful, like sharing words of encouragement. We should guard our speech by thinking before we talk, like checking your change before buying something at the market.

Class activity:
Pupils will practice giving compliments to classmates and write down kind words they can use this week.

Evaluation questions:
1. How can words be both helpful and harmful?
2. What does the Bible say about our speech?
3. Name one way to guard your tongue.
4. Give an example of healing words you can say to someone.

Summary:
Christians should use their words to build others up, not tear them down.

topics.title: Wealth and generosity
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain what it means to be rich toward God, identify ways to be generous, and list biblical teachings about wealth.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about the power of words. Today we will learn how God wants us to think about money and possessions.

Content:
Being rich toward God means using what we have to serve Him and help others. The rich man in the Bible who stored up all his grain was not wise because he did not share. The widow gave only two small coins but Jesus said she gave more than everyone because she gave all she had. Generous habits include sharing food with neighbors, giving to the poor, and supporting church work. Like planting palm kernels, generosity brings blessings in return.

Class activity:
Pupils will make a list of things they can share with others at school or home.

Evaluation questions:
1. What does it mean to be rich toward God?
2. Why was the widow's offering special to Jesus?
3. Name two ways you can be generous.
4. What does the Bible teach about storing up treasures?

Summary:
God values generosity more than wealth, and we should share what we have with others.

topics.title: Marriage and family God's way
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain the importance of honour and love in marriage, identify ways to show family devotion, and list biblical principles for family life.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about generosity. Today we will learn how God wants husbands and wives to love each other and how families should live together in peace.

Content:
God designed marriage to be between one man and one woman who love and honour each other. Husbands should love their wives like Christ loves the church, and wives should respect their husbands. Family devotion means praying together, reading the Bible, and showing love daily. Like the way we celebrate with family during New Yam festival, Christian families should celebrate God's love together. Children should obey their parents as a way of honouring God.

Class activity:
Pupils will interview their parents about how their family shows love and respect.

Evaluation questions:
1. What does the Bible say about love in marriage?
2. How can families show devotion to God?
3. Why is it important for children to obey their parents?
4. Give an example of honour in a family.

Summary:
God's plan for families is based on love, respect, and shared devotion to Him.

topics.title: Christian youth and purity
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain why purity is important for youth, identify ways to maintain boundaries, and list good qualities of Christian friends.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about marriage and family. Today we will learn how young Christians should live pure lives and choose good friends.

Content:
Purity means keeping your body, mind, and heart clean in God's sight. Young Christians should avoid bad things like immoral movies and bad language. Boundaries are rules that protect you, like not being alone with someone of the opposite gender in a private place. Good friends encourage you to do right, like when your friends remind you to study for exams. Like the way we avoid bad roads at night, youth should avoid situations that could lead to sin.

Class activity:
Pupils will create posters showing ways to stay pure and choose good friends.

Evaluation questions:
1. What does purity mean for Christian youth?
2. Why are boundaries important for young people?
3. What qualities should you look for in Christian friends?
4. How can youth resist peer pressure to do wrong?

Summary:
Young Christians should stay pure by making wise choices and surrounding themselves with good friends.

topics.title: Discernment
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain how to test every spirit, identify wise choices Christians should make, and list ways to discern good from evil.

Introduction:
Last week we learned about purity for youth. Today we will learn how Christians can know what is right and wrong in a world with many choices.

Content:
Discernment is the ability to tell what is good and what is bad, like a market woman who can tell ripe palm fruit from unripe. We test every spirit by seeing if it agrees with the Bible, like checking if money is real by looking at the watermark. Wise choices include praying before making decisions, seeking advice from godly people, and listening to the Holy Spirit. Like the way our grandparents use proverbs to teach wisdom, the Bible gives us guidance for making good choices.

Class activity:
Pupils will work in groups to solve scenarios requiring discernment and explain their choices.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is discernment?
2. How can Christians test if something is from God?
3. Name two ways to make wise choices.
4. Why is discernment important for Christians today?

Summary:
Christians should use discernment to make choices that please God in every situation.

topics.title: Revision and memory work
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to recite memory verses, answer questions from the term's lessons, and participate in a Bible quiz.

Introduction:
This week we will review all we have learned this term and practice some important Bible verses.

Content:
We will review the key points from each lesson this term, including the birth of the church, Paul's letters, persecution, faith and works, the tongue, wealth and generosity, marriage, purity, and discernment. Memory verses include James 1:22 about being doers of the word and Philippians 4:13 about doing all things through Christ who strengthens us. Like a farmer who reviews his work before harvest, we review our lessons to strengthen our understanding of God's word.

Class activity:
Pupils will participate in a Bible quiz competition in teams.

Evaluation questions:
1. Recite one memory verse from this term.
2. What is the most important lesson you learned this term?
3. Name three topics we studied this term.
4. How will you apply what you learned in your daily life?

Summary:
Reviewing helps us remember important lessons from God's word and apply them to our lives.
